name: Cellular Respiration
what: Covers the ATP-ADP energy shuttle, the structure of the mitochondrion, and the inputs, outputs, locations and ATP yields of glycolysis, the Krebs Cycle and the electron transport chain in aerobic respiration, as well as anaerobic fermentation in animals, plants and yeasts.
why: Cellular respiration explains how all living cells extract usable energy from glucose. Understanding its stages is essential for explaining how organisms respond to changing oxygen availability and how ATP is produced to power all cellular processes.

items.title: I can state the purpose of cellular respiration
items.what: Cellular respiration is a series of biochemical reactions in which glucose is broken down to produce ATP, the cell's primary energy currency. It occurs in all living cells and can proceed with oxygen (aerobic) or without it (anaerobic).
items.why: Distinguishing between the purpose of cellular respiration (making ATP) and the purpose of photosynthesis (making glucose) is a common point of confusion assessed in exams.
items.example: Muscle cells during exercise carry out aerobic cellular respiration to produce the ATP needed to power muscle contraction.

items.title: I can explain the function of the mitochondria
items.what: The mitochondrion is the site of the Krebs Cycle (in the matrix) and the electron transport chain (on the cristae of the inner membrane). It converts the chemical energy in pyruvate into ATP through these two stages of aerobic cellular respiration.
items.why: The mitochondrion is central to aerobic respiration and its structural features directly explain its function. This connection between structure and function is regularly assessed.
items.example: Cells that perform a lot of active transport, such as intestinal epithelial cells, contain large numbers of mitochondria because they require large amounts of ATP.

items.title: I can draw and label a mitochondrion and recall the function of its key structures
items.what: A mitochondrion has an outer membrane, inner membrane, cristae (folds of the inner membrane), matrix, ribosomes and DNA. The cristae increase surface area for the electron transport chain; the matrix contains enzymes for the Krebs Cycle.
items.why: Like the chloroplast, the mitochondrion is a high-priority diagram in VCE Biology. Labelling it correctly and linking each structure to a function is expected in assessment.
items.example: A mitochondrion with many deep cristae has a greater surface area for the electron transport chain, so more ATP can be produced per unit time compared to a mitochondrion with fewer cristae.

items.title: I can demonstrate an understanding of the energy shuttle and uses of ATP
items.what: ATP acts as an energy shuttle by storing energy in a high-energy bond between its second and third phosphate groups. When that bond is broken (ATP → ADP + Pi), energy is released for cellular processes. Energy is stored again when ADP is phosphorylated back to ATP.
items.why: The ATP-ADP cycle underpins every energy-requiring process in the cell. Understanding it is required for explaining how energy is transferred between the stages of cellular respiration and for answering questions about endergonic and exergonic reactions.
items.example: When a nerve cell fires an impulse, ATP is hydrolysed to ADP + Pi, releasing energy to power the sodium-potassium pump. The ADP is then recharged to ATP using energy from cellular respiration.

items.title: I can tabulate the inputs, outputs, location and ATP yield of each stage of aerobic cellular respiration
items.what: Glycolysis: cytosol, inputs glucose, outputs 2 pyruvate + 2 ATP + 2 NADH. Krebs Cycle: matrix, inputs 2 acetyl CoA + NAD+ + FAD+, outputs CO2 + 2 ATP + NADH + FADH2. Electron transport chain: cristae, inputs NADH + FADH2 + O2, outputs H2O + 26 or 28 ATP.
items.why: Tabulating all three stages with correct inputs, outputs, locations and ATP yields is a direct Study Design requirement and a very common exam question format.
items.example: In a table: Krebs Cycle — location: matrix of mitochondrion; inputs: acetyl CoA, NAD+, FAD+; outputs: CO2, NADH, FADH2; ATP yield: 2 per glucose.

items.title: I can outline what occurs during glycolysis, the Krebs Cycle and the electron transport chain
items.what: Glycolysis splits one glucose (6C) into two pyruvate (3C) molecules in the cytosol, producing 2 ATP and 2 NADH. The Krebs Cycle converts pyruvate (via acetyl CoA) in the matrix, releasing CO2 and producing NADH, FADH2 and 2 ATP. The electron transport chain uses H+ ions from NADH and FADH2 to drive ATP synthase on the cristae, producing up to 28 ATP and water.
items.why: Describing what occurs at each stage, rather than just listing inputs and outputs, is required for extended response questions and multi-mark explanations.
items.example: During the electron transport chain, electrons from NADH and FADH2 pass through a series of protein complexes on the cristae. The energy released pumps H+ across the membrane, and as H+ flow back through ATP synthase, ATP is produced. At the end of the chain, H+ and electrons combine with O2 to form water.

items.title: I can state the word equation and balanced chemical equation for aerobic cellular respiration
items.what: Word equation: glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water + energy (ATP). Balanced equation: C6H12O6 + 6O2 → 6CO2 + 6H2O + 30 or 32 ATP.
items.why: The overall equation for cellular respiration summarises all reactants and products and is frequently required in both short-answer and multiple-choice questions.
items.example: If a question asks what the products of aerobic cellular respiration are, the answer is carbon dioxide, water and ATP — not just energy, which is too vague for a biology response.

items.title: I can tabulate the inputs, outputs, location and difference in products of anaerobic fermentation in animals, plants and yeasts
items.what: All anaerobic fermentation begins with glycolysis (cytosol, glucose → 2 pyruvate + 2 ATP). In animals: pyruvate is converted to lactic acid in the cytosol. In plants and yeast: pyruvate is converted to ethanol and CO2 in the cytosol. Both pathways restore NAD+ so glycolysis can continue.
items.why: The difference in products between animal and yeast/plant fermentation is a specific Study Design requirement. It is regularly tested in short-answer format.
items.example: During intense sprint exercise, human muscle cells run short of oxygen and switch to lactic acid fermentation, producing lactic acid and 2 ATP per glucose. Yeast in bread dough under the same anaerobic conditions produces ethanol and CO2, causing the dough to rise.

items.title: I can state the word equation for anaerobic cellular respiration
items.what: For animals: glucose → lactic acid + 2 ATP. For plants and yeast: glucose → ethanol + carbon dioxide + 2 ATP.
items.why: Stating the correct word equation, including the correct products for the specific organism, is required for full marks in assessment. Mixing up lactic acid and ethanol is a common error.
items.example: If a question describes yeast fermenting sugar in a sealed container, the expected word equation is: glucose → ethanol + carbon dioxide + 2 ATP.
